pr.title: Do not lifetime-extend array/slice indices
pr.description:
When lowering non-overloaded indexing operations to MIR, this uses the temporary lifetime of the index expression for the index temporary, rather than applying the temporary lifetime of the indexing operation as a whole to the index.

For example, in
```rust
let x = &xs[i];
```
previously, the temporary containing the result of evaluating `i` would live until the end of the block due to the indexing operation being [lifetime-extended](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/destructors.html#temporary-lifetime-extension). Under this PR, the index temporary only lives to the end of the `let` statement because it uses the more precise temporary lifetime of the index expression.

I don't think this will affect semantics in an observable way, but the more precise `StorageDead` placement may slightly improve analysis/codegen performance.

r? mir
pr.author: dianne

processing.reason: The supplied PR (rust-lang/rust#147083) changes only where the MIR index temporary's StorageDead is placed: the index expression's own temp_lifetime is used instead of the indexing operation's possibly lifetime-extended temp_lifetime. The PR author explicitly states this is not expected to affect observable semantics; it delays StorageDead and slightly worsens analysis/codegen on the old path. The regression evidence is entirely MIR/NLL expectation diffs (moved StorageDead, changed region live-ranges), not a runtime value difference. No source-grounded original/transformed Rust function pair can be constructed whose defined, repeated executions produce different values under this rewrite without fabricating an unrelated semantic change (e.g. use-after-StorageDead/UB tricks or artificial return-value edits), which the task forbids. Therefore there is no valid runtime counterexample to validate.

analysis.incorrectTransformation: The historical transformation was: materialize the index expression with the indexing operation's `expr.temp_lifetime` (`self.as_temp(block, temp_lifetime, index, Mutability::Not)`) instead of with the index expression's own lifetime (`self.thir[index].temp_lifetime`). This over-extended the index temporary's lifetime whenever the indexing operation was lifetime-extended. It is an imprecise temporary-lifetime choice rather than a confirmed semantic miscompile: the PR description says it is not thought to affect semantics observably, but it delayed `StorageDead` and could slightly hurt analysis/codegen performance. The corrected transformation keeps the same fresh index temporary and bounds check but uses the index expression's `temp_lifetime`, so the index temporary dies at the end of the `let` statement.
analysis.inputDomain: Rust source containing non-overloaded indexing of arrays or slices, where the index expression is materialized into a fresh temporary and the indexing operation's temporary lifetime differs from the index expression's temporary lifetime. The canonical shape is a lifetime-extended indexing borrow such as `let x = &xs[i];`; regression tests also cover slice indexing such as `_2 = &(*_1)[_3];` and wider indexing patterns. Use both panic-abort and panic-unwind MIR configurations. A useful source pair should keep the same indexing operation and differ only in whether the indexing operation's temporary lifetime is extended (for example, an indexing borrow assigned to a `let` versus a context where the indexing result is not lifetime-extended), so the observable compiler difference is the placement of the index temporary's `StorageDead` and the NLL region ranges.
analysis.originalLogic: Before the PR, non-overloaded array/slice indexing lowering passed the indexing operation's temporary lifetime (`expr.temp_lifetime`) into `as_temp` when materializing the index expression. That made the fresh index temporary inherit the lifetime of the indexing operation as a whole. Thus in a lifetime-extended indexing expression such as `let x = &xs[i];`, the temporary containing the evaluated index `i` lived until the end of the block, and its `StorageDead` appeared at the end of the block rather than at the end of the `let` statement.
pitfalls: Do not treat this as a confirmed bug fix or a semantic miscompile: the PR says the change is not expected to affect semantics observably.
Do not extend the index temporary to the indexing operation's lifetime; its lifetime must follow the index expression's own temporary lifetime.

Do not remove the fresh index temporary or reuse it: the source comment states a fresh temporary ensures the index never changes and that the retagging transformation for Stacked Borrows relies on this.
Do not shorten the index temporary so far that it expires before the bounds check or before the indexing operation uses it; only move its `StorageDead` after its last use.
The test diffs move `StorageDead` for the index local earlier while leaving unrelated locals' `StorageDead` in place; do not conflate this with GVN value numbering or with post-copy overwrites.
The NLL region ranges change as a consequence of the earlier `StorageDead`; these are expected test updates, not evidence of a different optimization pass.
Panic-abort and panic-unwind both need checking because the MIR control-flow and `StorageDead` placement differ around unwinding paths.
preconditions: The indexing operation is non-overloaded array/slice indexing, so it is lowered directly rather than through an overloaded `Index` call.
The index expression is lowered through `as_temp`, creating a fresh temporary so the index cannot change later and Stacked Borrows retagging remains valid.
The indexing operation has a temporary lifetime that can be longer than the index expression's own temporary lifetime, as with `let x = &xs[i];`.
The test configuration dumps MIR or NLL region information; the optimization is visible as moved `StorageDead` instructions and changed region live-ranges, not necessarily as runtime output.
analysis.summary: Historical Rust MIR-lowering PR makes the temporary holding an array/slice index use the index expression's own temporary lifetime instead of the indexing operation's lifetime. The prior behavior lifetime-extended the index temporary to the end of the block whenever the indexing operation was lifetime-extended, e.g. in `let x = &xs[i];`. The PR moves the index temporary's `StorageDead` earlier, to the end of the `let` statement, and updates GVN/NLL MIR expectations accordingly. The author explicitly says this is not believed to change observable semantics; it is a precision/codegen-improvement optimization. Knowledge is attached to GVN because the supplied regression evidence is `tests/mir-opt/gvn.*.GVN.*.diff`, even though the lowering change itself is in MIR building before GVN.
analysis.testStrategy: Use compile-time MIR tests rather than runtime execution claims. Start from `tests/mir-opt/gvn.dereference_indexing` and `tests/mir-opt/gvn.wide_ptr_same_provenance` in both panic-abort and panic-unwind modes, plus `tests/mir-opt/issue_91633.fun.built.after.mir` and the 32-bit/64-bit `tests/mir-opt/nll/region_subtyping_basic` dumps. Construct source pairs with non-overloaded indexing where the indexing operation is or is not lifetime-extended, and compare the generated MIR: the index temporary's `StorageDead` should occur immediately after the indexing statement/`let` in the optimized revision, not at the end of the block. Check that the bounds check still precedes the index temporary's death, that the fresh index temporary is preserved, and that NLL live-ranges shrink accordingly. Do not assert runtime semantic changes; assert MIR/StorageDead and region-range differences only. No compiler was built here, so these are inspection-based expectations from the supplied test diffs.
analysis.trigger: Lowering a non-overloaded array/slice indexing expression when the index expression is a temporary and the indexing operation is lifetime-extended, especially `let x = &xs[i];` or MIR such as `_2 = &(*_1)[_3];`. Under the old lowering the index temporary's `StorageDead` was placed at the end of the block; the optimization moves it to the end of the `let` statement.
